questions.question: Describe the Battle of Delville Wood and its significance.
questions.expected_answer: The 1st South African Infantry Brigade, white volunteers under Brigadier-General Henry Lukin, was ordered on 15 July 1916, during the Somme offensive, to take Delville Wood near Longueval and hold it at all costs. About 3 150 men entered, took most of the wood, but faced six days of counter-attacks and intense bombardment from three sides, in mud and destroyed forest. When relieved on 20 July, only about 780 answered the roll call. Private William Faulds won the Victoria Cross. The 1926 memorial made it a symbol of white South African sacrifice; in 2016 it was rededicated to all South Africans who served.

questions.question: Describe the sinking of the SS Mendi.
questions.expected_answer: The troopship SS Mendi carried 802 men of the 5th Battalion of the South African Native Labour Contingent from Cape Town towards France. In fog off the Isle of Wight early on 21 February 1917, the much larger SS Darro, travelling too fast, struck her, and she sank in about twenty minutes; many men were trapped, most could not swim, the water was icy and the Darro did not help. 607 SANLC men, 9 officers and NCOs and 30 crew died, 616 South Africans and 646 in all. Oral tradition records Reverend Isaac Wauchope Dyobha urging courage and the men's death drill; the Darro's captain lost his licence for one year.

questions.question: Explain why Delville Wood and the Mendi were remembered differently.
questions.expected_answer: South Africa's forces were segregated: black South Africans served as unarmed labourers in the SANLC, coloured South Africans in the Cape Corps. Delville Wood, fought by white soldiers, was honoured with a national memorial from 1926. SANLC members were denied the British War and Victory Medals, and the Mendi had no national memorial, though black communities remembered it through Mendi Day, churches and S. E. K. Mqhayi's poem. After 1994, Mandela and Queen Elizabeth II unveiled a Soweto memorial in 1995, the Order of Mendi Decoration for Bravery and SAS Mendi were created, and Delville Wood was rededicated in 2016. Memory reflects values and power.
